india: Chile peppers reached India in the 1500s, carried by Portuguese trade.
mexico: Chile peppers were domesticated in Mexico.
nasha: NASHA would cook with chile from both kitchens: dried guajillo and ancho beside Indian red chiles, each for a different job.
note: Origin in Mexico is well established. The exact route and year into India are still debated, so we state neither.

india: Many Indian sauces start by toasting and grinding spices, seeds or nuts.
mexico: Many Mexican sauces, including mole, toast and grind chiles, seeds and nuts.
nasha: Toasted spices and seeds run through the Core 5, from curry leaf to dried chile. It is our own composition, and untested.
note: The similarity is one of technique. We found no evidence of a shared history and we do not claim one.

india: Tamarind, lime, yogurt and pickles bring sourness.
mexico: Lime, vinegar, tamarind and pickled onion bring sourness.
nasha: Tamarind-chile glaze, lime slaw, pickled onion: acid to balance fat and heat.
note: Both cuisines use tamarind. How it reached Mexico is unresolved, so we make no origin claim.

india: The tandoor: a hot clay oven for marinated meats, vegetables and breads.
mexico: The comal and the grill: hot surfaces for tortillas, vegetables and meats.
nasha: The paneer tikka taco borrows tandoori-style char for a corn tortilla. It is our own dish, and its heat source is unresolved.
note: Two independent cooking systems. We compare them; we do not claim a historical link.

mexico: Tortillas of corn, and flour tortillas in the north.
nasha: Corn tortillas carry the fillings; flatbread logic returns in the quesadilla.
note: A human story is documented: Punjabi men and Mexican women formed families in California in the early 1900s. It is diaspora history, not a trade of recipes.

india: Rice dishes such as biryani, steamed in a sealed pot.
mexico: Maize in all its forms; rice also appears in Mexican meals.
nasha: Biryani is a later idea, waiting for a cook who can judge it. We will not use a regional name unless it is earned.
note: We make no claim about origins of biryani or of dum cooking; the stories are folklore.

india: Dal: lentils simmered long and finished with spiced butter or oil.
mexico: Frijoles: beans simmered long, often with epazote.
nasha: Our designed Dal-Frijol Dip is built on this shared patience. It is our own dish.
note: Both are slow-simmered staples. Nothing more is claimed.

india: Fermented drinks are documented in Indian texts, including a grain drink in the Rigveda.
mexico: Chemical residue at Teotihuacan (about AD 200 to 550) is the earliest direct evidence of pulque found so far.
nasha: Beer would be our fermentation: a European-style craft beer program, not a revival of either tradition.
note: These are parallel human inventions with no established connection.
